Cited by [LIT-970](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-970.md) as Ziyin (2024). The source of [THEORY-213](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-213.md). |
| [LIT-1044](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1044.md) v2 | Why Do Better Loss Functions Lead to Less Transferable Features? | Kornblith, Chen, Lee & Norouzi (2020; NeurIPS 2021). Nine training objectives for ResNet-50 on ImageNet: seven beat softmax cross-entropy significantly, by up to 0.9 points top-1, and all eight alternatives yield fixed penultimate features that transfer worse to eight new-class datasets, by linear and k-NN readout. Each raises penultimate-layer class separation R² (one minus within-class over total cosine distance), and mean linear transfer falls with R² across losses (Spearman ρ = −0.93) and along a cosine-softmax temperature sweep. The losses differ only in the last third of the network, and full fine-tuning removes the gap. | Active — read 2026-10-14 ([NOTE-762](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-762.md)) in full; worth reading as the record's one direct measurement of what class separation in the last layers costs off the trained task. Across nine objectives for ResNet-50 on ImageNet, those that beat softmax cross-entropy all raise penultimate-layer class separation (R² 0.349 → up to 0.845), and mean linear transfer to eight new-class datasets falls with it (Spearman ρ = −0.93; 75.9% for softmax, 48.3% for squared error). Cosine-softmax temperature moves both on one knob. The losses differ only in the last third of the network, and full fine-tuning erases the transfer gap. Read it knowing that the networks are early-stopped at 91.6–93.6% training accuracy, so this is relative within-class variance and not terminal-phase neural collapse; that the cost is for new classes, while on shifted ImageNet test sets with the same classes the more separated losses do slightly better (Table C.2); and that it is one dataset, two architectures and a correlation across losses, with one within-loss sweep. Filed as [THEORY-246](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-246.md). |
| [LIT-1052](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1052.md) | Calibration for the (Computationally-Identifiable) Masses | Hébert-Johnson, Kim, Reingold and Rothblum (2018), ICML; arXiv 1711.08513. A predictor is α-multicalibrated on a collection C of subpopulations if, within every set S in C, the individuals given (roughly) the same prediction v have true probabilities averaging within α of v, except on an α-fraction of S. For any C whose sets have size at least γN, a simple iterative patching algorithm reaches multicalibration from O(log\|C\|/α^{11/2}γ^{3/2}) samples in time linear in \|C\|, and the result is a circuit only O(s/α⁴γ) in size when the sets of C are computed by size-s circuits. Learning it is equivalent, up to polynomial factors, to weak agnostic learning of C, so it is hard for rich C under cryptographic assumptions. Calibrating any predictor h on its own level sets as well as on C costs at most 6α in squared error. All guarantees are relative to the benchmark p*, which is itself defined relative to the features available, and they hold only for large sets; the paper offers no uniqueness for the predictor and does not state a theorem in indistinguishability form. | Active — read in full 2026-10-15 from the authors' arXiv preprint, latest version v2 of 16 March 2018 (arxiv.org/pdf/1711.08513, 40 pp.); the ICML version (PMLR 80:1939–1948, proceedings.mlr.press/v80/hebert-johnson18a/hebert-johnson18a.pdf, with a supplement) was fetched and its definitions and theorem statements compared, not read in full. Worth reading as the source definition of multicalibration: calibration required on every set in a collection C of large, efficiently identifiable subpopulations; a patching algorithm that reaches it from O(log\|C\|/α^{11/2}γ^{3/2}) samples in time linear in \|C\|, with a circuit of size O(s/α⁴γ); learning it equivalent to weak agnostic learning of C, and so hard for rich C under cryptographic assumptions; and calibration on any predictor's level sets at almost no cost in squared error. Its multi-AE (accuracy in expectation on every S in C) is what later work calls multiaccuracy; the paper does not use that word. For [QUESTION-103](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-103.md) it supplies adequacy relative to a class of observers in correlation form (a violation is a set in C correlating with the residual), but it states no indistinguishability theorem, no distinguishing advantage and nothing from signal detection; that framing is Dwork et al.'s ([LIT-1068](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1068.md)). For [CLAIM-152](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-152.md) it is consistent and adds a second relativity: adequacy is relative to the outcome, to the features through p*, and to the class C, and even with all three fixed the adequate predictor is not unique. For [QUESTION-104](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-104.md) it gives a formal instance of budget-relative sufficiency in which representing an adequate predictor is cheap (only modestly larger than the observer class) while finding one can be hard, but it has no notion of an optimal partition and does not show one changing with the budget. |
| [LIT-1063](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1063.md) | Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally can be More Effective than Scaling Model Parameters | Snell, Lee, Xu and Kumar (2024, arXiv 2408.03314; ICLR 2025). On MATH with PaLM 2-S*, which way of spending test-time compute works best (beam search against a process reward model versus best-of-N; sequential self-revision versus parallel sampling) depends on how hard the question is for the base model, and choosing the method per difficulty bin matches best-of-N with up to about 4× less test-time compute (the discussion says 2–4×). In a FLOPs-matched comparison with a ~14× larger model, the extra test-time compute a small model may spend is set by R, the ratio of total inference tokens to pretraining tokens: when R is small the larger model's pretraining cost buys many samples per query and test-time compute wins on easy and medium questions; when R is large the budget per query falls toward the parameter ratio and the larger model wins, always on the hardest questions. Difficulty estimation (2048 samples per question) and verifier and revision-model finetuning are not counted in the compute, R is an aggregate token ratio with no term for which queries recur, and the evidence is one model family on one benchmark of 500 test questions. | Active — read in full 2026-10-15 from the arXiv preprint (arxiv.org/pdf/2408.03314, v1 of 2024-08-06, the only arXiv version) and from the ICLR 2025 conference version, open access in the ICLR proceedings (proceedings.iclr.cc, retitled "... than Scaling Parameters for Reasoning"), which is a revision not posted to arXiv: it charges verifier calls to inference FLOPs, which halves the stated R values (0.16/0.79/22 become 0.08/0.40/11) at unchanged budgets, and adds a verifier-quality check. Worth reading as the standard empirical case that the best use of inference compute depends on how hard a question is for the base model, and that choosing the method per difficulty bin matches best-of-N with up to about 4× less test-time compute on MATH with PaLM 2-S*, before counting the 2048-sample difficulty estimate. For [QUESTION-095](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-095.md) it shows a FLOPs-matched amortization model: a ~14× larger model's extra pretraining is a fixed cost spread over all inference, so the per-query test-time budget it buys scales as M + 3(M − 1)/R, with R the ratio of inference to pretraining tokens; test-time compute wins at low R on easy and medium questions and loses at high R and on the hardest questions at every R. R is aggregate inference volume, not a count of recurring queries; the larger model's per-token cost is a retrieval-cost term; query predictability appears as difficulty but its cost is not counted; staleness and erosion are absent. |
| [LIT-1068](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1068.md) | Outcome Indistinguishability | Dwork, Kim, Reingold, Rothblum and Yona (2021), STOC; arXiv 2011.13426. A predictor p̃ is outcome indistinguishable (OI) relative to a class A of distinguishers when no A ∈ A can tell an individual with Nature's outcome from the same individual with an outcome drawn from Ber(p̃_i). The paper sets out four levels by how much access the distinguisher has to p̃: none, the prediction on the sampled individual, oracle queries, or the code. The lower two levels are equivalent to multi-accuracy and multi-calibration over closely related classes. At those levels OI predictors exist with size O(s/ε²), whatever Nature's complexity. At the oracle level, under fine-grained hardness of clique counting or BPP ≠ PSPACE, some efficient distinguisher classes force any OI predictor to be nearly as expensive as Nature's own predictor. That gives a strict separation between oracle access and sample access. OI never requires p̃ ≈ p*. A predictor is good only relative to A, and with the paper's construction a weak A gives a coarse predictor that a richer A would refute. The paper covers binary outcomes, a fixed representation of individuals and single samples (multi-sample OI is left mostly to future work). | Active — read in full 2026-10-15 from the arXiv preprint, arXiv:2011.13426v1 (arxiv.org/pdf/2011.13426, 61 pp.), the only arXiv version. The STOC 2021 version of record (doi:10.1145/3406325.3451064) was not read; its only open copies are submitted versions (arXiv, MIT DSpace). The recurrence algebra of Theorems 5.9–5.10 and the proof of Proposition 6.3 were checked for structure only. Worth reading as the source of outcome indistinguishability. A predictor is adequate relative to a class A of distinguishers when none can tell its sampled outcomes from Nature's. The paper sets out four levels by the distinguisher's access to the predictor (none, the sampled prediction, oracle queries, the code). It proves the lower two equivalent to multi-accuracy and multi-calibration and gives OI predictors of size O(s/ε²) whatever Nature's complexity. At the oracle level it gives conditional hardness (clique counting, or BPP ≠ PSPACE): cheap distinguishers with query access can force any OI predictor to be about as costly as Nature's own. For [QUESTION-103](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-103.md) it supplies the formal half: distinguishing advantage is the ROC quantity, and with all subset distinguishers it becomes statistical distance. It says nothing about SDT, criteria or ideal-observer efficiency, and adds that access as well as budget sets an observer's power. For [CLAIM-152](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-152.md) it is an instance of adequacy relative to the observer class with the target held fixed, with no uniqueness or minimality of the predictor. For [QUESTION-104](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-104.md) it shows a restricted class accepting a coarser model (p̃ ≡ 1/2 where Nature's two halves are computationally indistinguishable), but at the oracle and code levels a bounded observer need not be satisfied by a cheap model. |
| [LIT-1069](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1069.md) | Scaling Scaling Laws with Board Games | Jones (2021), arXiv 2104.03113. Training AlphaZero on Hex at board sizes 3×3 to 9×9, the best Elo reachable for a given training compute follows one change-point curve across sizes: an incline of about 500 Elo per tenfold of training compute, with the compute for perfect play rising about 7× and the compute to leave random play about 4× per added board row, and fits on small boards predicting larger ones. On 9×9 only, train-time and test-time (tree-search) compute substitute at a fixed rate: at equal Elo, each 10× of train-time compute removes about 15× of test-time compute (fit: log test = −1.2·log train + 0.004·Elo + 29), down to a one-node search, over roughly 1e14–1e16 FLOPS-seconds of training. The trade is an iso-performance curve for a single search; the paper never counts how many games or moves the trained agent will play, so it does not price amortization, and it does not state the unit of test-time compute. One game, small boards, Elo anchored to a perfect player, and no uncertainty on the fitted trade-off coefficients. | Active — read in full 2026-10-15 from the author's arXiv preprint, version 2 of 2021-04-15, the latest (arxiv.org/pdf/2104.03113v2; v1 diffed against it, same methods and numbers). Worth reading as a clean small-scale scaling law in problem size as well as compute: AlphaZero on Hex, boards 3×3 to 9×9, one change-point frontier of about 500 Elo per tenfold of training compute, with the compute for perfect play rising about 7× per added board row and fits on small boards predicting larger ones. For [QUESTION-095](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-095.md) it shows that, on 9×9 at fixed Elo, training and tree-search compute substitute along a straight log–log line, about 15× less search per 10× more training (fit: log test = −1.2·log train + 0.004·Elo + 29), over roughly 1e14–1e16 FLOPS-seconds of training and down to a one-node search; it does not count the games or moves the trained agent will play, or define the unit of test-time compute, so it prices the iso-performance substitution but not amortization, and has no terms for query shift, staleness or erosion of search. |
| [LIT-1070](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1070.md) | Beyond Chinchilla-Optimal: Accounting for Inference in Language Model Scaling Laws | Sardana, Portes, Doubov and Frankle (2024, ICML; arXiv 2401.00448). Fixing a target pre-training loss and adding inference FLOPs (2N per token over a known lifetime demand D_inf) to training FLOPs (6N per token), the compute-minimising model is smaller and trained on more data than Chinchilla-optimal, increasingly so as D_inf approaches and exceeds the training-set size; the optimum has no closed form and is found numerically. The savings are modest in FLOPs (for a 30B-Chinchilla-quality model with 10^13 inference tokens, 28% by training 13.6B on 2.84× the data) and larger in dollars once inference's low hardware utilisation is priced in (17% to 58% in the paper's examples). 47 training runs (150M–6B parameters, 10–10,000 tokens per parameter) find loss still falling at extreme ratios, but more slowly than Chinchilla-fitted laws predict, so the formula overstates the gain from long training. Demand is assumed known before training and fixed given quality; there is no term for uncertainty, discounting, obsolescence or a model being replaced. | Active — read in full 2026-10-15 from the authors' arXiv preprint v3 (arxiv.org/pdf/2401.00448v3, 14 Apr 2025), which is the ICML 2024 paper (PMLR 235, also fetched from proceedings.mlr.press/v235/sardana24a.html and diffed: same equations, tables and numbers, small wording edits); v1 (2023-12-31) is an earlier two-author NeurIPS 2023 workshop version without the experiments. Worth reading as the worked case of choosing how much to precompute by expected use: fixing quality, it adds lifetime inference FLOPs (2N per token) to training FLOPs (6N per token), finds the optimum numerically (no closed form), and shows the optimal model shrinking and training longer as demand grows (30B-Chinchilla quality with 10^13 inference tokens: 13.6B on 2.84× the data, 28% fewer FLOPs; in dollars, with inference at 1% utilisation, savings of 17% to 58%), with 47 training runs up to 10,000 tokens per parameter showing quality still improving but more slowly than the fitted law predicts. For [QUESTION-095](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-095.md) it supplies expected reuse and a non-zero per-use cost as explicit terms, and nothing for staleness, uncertainty about demand (assumed known before training) or erosion; for [CLAIM-303](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-303.md) it instantiates the break-even n > F/(c_r − c_a − u) with u = 0, and shows the choice as a continuous dial tied by a production function rather than a file-or-not decision. |
| [LIT-1071](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1071.md) | Resource-rational analysis: Understanding human cognition as the optimal use of limited computational resources | Lieder and Griffiths (2020; online 2019), BBS 43. Resource rationality defines the right cognitive mechanism as the one, among those a brain can execute, that maximizes expected utility of its result minus the expected opportunity cost of the time and resources it uses (Eq. 3), averaged over the environments consistent with what is known (Eq. 4); resource-rational analysis is a five-step iterate-and-refine method for deriving process models from that objective. The objective is per episode. It has no separate terms for storing a result, retrieving it later, or its going stale: the value of what a computation leaves behind is folded into the utility of the episode's result, and the cost of finding the heuristic in the first place is assigned to evolution and learning and left out. Reuse appears only in the review, qualitatively: habits as reused action sequences, Dasgupta et al. 2018's memorized hypotheses, Howes et al. 2016's memory-load choice (the review's "memorize-or-look-up"), and "cognitive prostheses". The framework is offered as a methodological device, not a claim that people are optimal. | Active — read in full 2026-10-15 from the publisher's typeset PDF of the whole BBS treatment (target article pp. 1–16, Authors' Response pp. 45–51, and the commentaries of Bates, Sims & Jacobs, Dimov, Dingemanse, and Ma & Woodford; the other 21 commentaries searched by keyword only), posted by the Griffiths lab at cocosci.princeton.edu/papers/lieder_resource.pdf. Unpaywall and OpenAlex list it as closed. Worth reading as the standard statement of resource rationality: the best mechanism a brain can run is the one that maximizes expected utility of its result minus the expected opportunity cost of the time and resources it takes (Eqs. 3–4), and the five-step method that derives process models from that. For [QUESTION-095](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-095.md) it shows that one objective can cover computing, remembering and retrieving, and it groups habits, memorized inferences (Dasgupta et al. 2018) and how much to hold in memory (Howes et al. 2016, which the review calls a memorize-or-look-up trade) under it. But the objective is per episode and has no separate terms for precompute, storage, retrieval or staleness. It leaves the cost of finding a heuristic out on purpose, as already paid by evolution and learning. Offloading to the world appears only in Dingemanse's commentary, which the authors accept as a frontier. For [CLAIM-303](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-303.md) it supplies the general benefit-minus-cost form the break-even condition fits, and no support for the claim's staleness term. |

Training a sum of many parameterized units by gradient descent is, in the many-particle limit, a Wasserstein gradient flow on the measure over unit parameters; under homogeneity and support conditions, limits of the flow are global minimizers. No NOTE is filed. |

Identifies conditions under which selection on ecological interactions is equivalent to unsupervised connectionist learning, so that a community with no community-level selection can organize itself, habituate to past environments and recall them. | Deferred — filed 2026-10-18, not read. | [LIT-1258](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1258.md) v2 | Exact and Soft Successive Refinement of the Information Bottleneck | Charvin, Catenacci Volpi & Polani (Entropy 2023). Defines successive refinement for the information bottleneck in single-letter form: a coarse optimum T₁ can be extended to a fine optimum (T₁, S). This holds iff some pair of optima forms the chain X → T₂ → T₁, iff the coarse encoder is a garbling of the fine one, and, when the fine decoder is injective, iff the coarse decoder points lie in the convex hull of the fine ones. That last form gives a linear-programming test. Refinability is proved for binary X and Y, for Y a function of X, and (from a cited semigroup result) for jointly Gaussian variables. Numerically, for 3×3 and larger random sources, the hull test on computed optima often fails, especially below the second bifurcation. The loss, measured by unique information, stayed under 5.4% of I(X; T₁, T₂). The failures are not certified, since global optimality and uniqueness of the optima are left as a conjecture. | Active — read 2026-10-20 ([NOTE-981](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-981.md)) in full, from the published version in the University of Hertfordshire Research Archive; worth reading for the single-letter definition of successive refinement for the information bottleneck and its equivalent forms (Proposition 1: some pair of optimal encoders forms the Markov chain X → T₂ → T₁; Proposition 8: the coarse encoder is a Blackwell garbling of the fine one); for the convex-hull test (Proposition 4: with an injective fine decoder, refinement holds iff every decoder point q(X\|t₁) lies in the convex hull of the q(X\|t₂)), checkable by a linear programme; for proofs of refinability when X and Y are both binary, when Y is a function of X, and for jointly Gaussian variables (the last resting on Kline and Palmer's semigroup result); and for soft refinement measured by unique information. Read it knowing that the linear programme tests the particular optima a solver returns, so that a failed test certifies nothing unless the optima are globally optimal and unique, which the paper leaves as Conjecture 1 and calls its own figures "mere numerical proxies" (Appendix D); that its evidence that refinement fails is therefore numerical and uncertified, with no count of how many sampled distributions failed; that the unique information computed is an upper bound on the soft measure for the same reason; that the deep-learning reading of §4.2 is speculative; and that the commentary on Proposition 8 swaps its points (ii) and (iii). |
| [LIT-1261](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1261.md) v2 | On the Spectral Bias of Neural Networks | Rahaman et al. (2019; arXiv 2018). Proves, for compactly supported ReLU networks, that the Fourier transform falls as k^(−d−1) in almost every direction and no slower than k^(−2). Shows by experiment that a deep ReLU network fits low frequencies before high ones, even when the high ones are ten times stronger, and that its high-frequency components are the least robust to parameter noise. Shows that on a curve embedded in the plane, high latent frequencies are fitted more easily as the embedding gets longer and more convoluted. | Active — read 2026-10-20 ([NOTE-983](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-983.md)) in full; worth reading for the experiment in which a ReLU network fits low frequencies before high ones even when the high ones are ten times stronger ([THEORY-759](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-759.md)), for the Fourier analysis of piecewise-linear networks ([THEORY-761](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-761.md)), and for the observation that the frequencies that are hard to learn depend on how the data's manifold is embedded. Read it knowing that its theorem is proved only for compactly supported networks, that the link from the theorem to the order of learning is an upper bound on speed and not a proof of order, that the volume result in Appendix D does not follow, and that its "manifold complexity" is confounded with the curve's length. |
| [LIT-1309](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1309.md) v2 | A Theory of Usable Information Under Computational Constraints | Xu, Zhao, Song, Stewart & Ermon (2020). Predictive V-information, H_V(Y) − H_V(Y \| X) with the conditional entropies taken as the least expected log loss over a predictive family V, is the information about Y that a predictor restricted to V can use. It recovers Shannon mutual information when V is unrestricted and the coefficient of determination for linear-Gaussian V, is non-negative and zero under independence, can be asymmetric, can be raised by computing on X, and can be estimated with PAC guarantees from the Rademacher complexity of V. | Active — read 2026-10-21 ([NOTE-1048](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1048.md)) in full, from arXiv:2002.10689v1, the ICLR 2020 camera-ready; worth reading as the usable-information literature the record lacked: it defines predictive V-information, the information a predictor restricted to a family V can extract, shows that computation can create it (so the data-processing inequality fails for it), and bounds its estimation error by the Rademacher complexity of V ([THEORY-846](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-846.md), [THEORY-840](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-840.md)). Read it knowing that the failure of the data-processing inequality is shown by informal examples (decryption, feature learning), not by a theorem, that V-information is not bounded by Shannon information unless V's input-free predictions include the true marginal (the record's counterexample, [THEORY-846](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-846.md)), that Proposition 1.2's "mean absolute deviation" is the deviation about the geometric median, and that the experiments are small. |
| [LIT-1336](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1336.md) v2 | Performative Prediction | Perdomo, Zrnic, Mendler-Dünner & Hardt (2020). When a deployed prediction changes the distribution of the outcomes it predicts, define performative stability (a model optimal for the distribution it induces) and performative optimality (least risk on the distribution it induces); show they can differ; prove that with a smooth, strongly convex loss and a distribution map ε-Lipschitz in Wasserstein distance, retraining converges to a unique stable point when ε < γ/β, that each condition is needed, and that stable points lie within 2L_zε/γ of optima. | Active — read 2026-10-21 ([NOTE-1044](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1044.md)) in full, from arXiv:2002.06673v4; worth reading for the split between performative stability (optimal for the distribution one's own deployment induces, the fixed point of retraining) and performative optimality, for the exact conditions under which retraining converges to a unique stable point (smooth, strongly convex loss and ε < γ/β, each shown necessary; [THEORY-861](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-861.md)), and for the bound 2L_zε/γ between stable points and optima ([THEORY-839](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-839.md)). Read it knowing that its conditions hold in its own simulation only at the smallest ε, that the distribution map depends on the current model alone, and that it says nothing about how to reach the optimum. |
| [LIT-1411](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1411.md) | Theory on Mixture-of-Experts in Continual Learning | Li, Lin, Duan, Liang & Shroff (2024; ICLR 2025). The first theoretical analysis of mixture-of-experts in continual learning, in overparameterized linear regression. The MoE diversifies its experts to specialize in different tasks while the router learns to send each task to the right expert and balance load. Unlike the static setting, convergence requires stopping gating-network updates after enough rounds. Explicit expressions are given for expected forgetting and generalization error; more experts need more rounds to converge and may not help. Experiments extend the insights to deep networks. | Deferred — filed 2026-10-23, not read. Registered from the owner's exchange of 2026-10-23, "Framework Overview Request". No NOTE is filed. |

Simplifies mixture-of-experts routing to a single expert per token (the Switch Transformer), reducing communication and computation, with training techniques for its instabilities that allow large sparse models to be trained, for the first time, in bfloat16. Up to 7x pre-training speedups over T5-Base and T5-Large at equal compute, gains across 101 languages over mT5-Base, and trillion-parameter models with a 4x speedup over T5-XXL. | Deferred — filed 2026-10-23, not read. An unbalanced expert load causes routing collapse or overhead, and the usual auxiliary balancing loss adds interference gradients that hurt performance. Loss-Free Balancing instead adds an expert-wise bias to routing scores before top-K selection and updates each bias from the expert's recent load. On MoE models up to 3B parameters trained on up to 200B tokens it gives both better performance and better balance than auxiliary-loss control. | Deferred — filed 2026-10-23, not read. | [LIT-1484](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1484.md) | The Hive Mind is a Single Reinforcement Learning Agent | Soma, Bouteiller, Hamann and Beltrame show that in an infinite, well-mixed population, imitation of success has the expected update of a single Cross Learning bandit agent, and the weighted voter model of the honey-bee waggle dance the expected update of "Maynard-Cross Learning", π_a ← π_a + (r_k / v^π)(1[a = k] − π_a), which is the Maynard-Smith replicator dynamic. Each member is one parallel action sample of the population's policy, and the members themselves do not learn. Simulations, qualitative by the authors' account, show the result surviving moderate swarm and neighbourhood sizes, and finite populations losing options for good. | Active — read in full 2026-10-24 ([NOTE-1132](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1132.md)) from arXiv v6 (21 July 2026, CC BY 4.0); worth reading as a proved aggregation result: in an infinite, well-mixed population, two imitation rules with no individual learning have the expected update of a single bandit-learning agent. Imitation of success gives Cross Learning (the Taylor replicator dynamic), the honey-bee weighted voter model gives what the authors call Maynard-Cross Learning (the Maynard-Smith replicator dynamic). The macro-agent is a stateless bandit policy over the members' types. The biological model is deliberately partial, the simulations qualitative, and pure imitation has no way back once a type is lost or the environment changes. |
| [LIT-1501](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1501.md) | A selection-mutation model for Q-learning in multi-agent systems | Tuyls, Verbeeck & Lenaerts (2003). Derives the continuous-time dynamics of Boltzmann Q-learning in two-player stateless matrix games, as later restated by Kaisers & Tuyls: ẋ_i = x_i α(τ⁻¹[(Ay)_i − x·Ay] − log x_i + Σ_k x_k log x_k), a replicator (selection) term plus an entropy (mutation) term, linking exploration in reinforcement learning to mutation in evolutionary game theory. Summary drawn from the abstract and from Kaisers & Tuyls 2010, not from the paper. | Unavailable — filed 2026-10-24 for the owner's question how the record stands on multi-agent reinforcement learning; a reading was attempted the same day and failed on access. The ACM Digital Library (doi:10.1145/860575.860687) answered every request from this client with a Cloudflare challenge (403). Unpaywall and OpenAlex list no open copy. The repository records OpenAlex names hold no file this client could reach: the VUB repository (biblio.vub.ac.be) page is a script-only catalogue entry, ULB's DI-fusion record shows no attached full text, the Hasselt document server returned 503 and a search result describes its record as "No Fulltext", and CiteSeerX reset the connection. Web searches found no author copy. The model the paper derives is read instead through Kaisers & Tuyls 2010 ([LIT-1511](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1511.md), [NOTE-1140](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1140.md)), which restates its equation and shows that it describes frequency-adjusted, not plain, Q-learning. It stays Unavailable until a copy is supplied. No NOTE is filed. |
| [LIT-1503](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1503.md) | QMIX: Monotonic Value Function Factorisation for Deep Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning | Rashid et al. represent a team's joint action-value Q_tot as a mixing of per-agent values Q_a(τ^a, u^a) constrained by ∂Q_tot/∂Q_a ≥ 0, with non-negative mixing weights produced from the global state by hypernetworks. Monotonicity makes the joint argmax the profile of individual argmaxes, so execution is decentralised and maximisation is linear in the number of agents. It represents more than a sum (VDN), learning the optimal policy of a two-step game VDN misses, and beat VDN and independent Q-learning on six StarCraft II maps; it cannot represent joint values in which an agent's best action depends on the others'. | Active — read in full 2026-10-24 ([NOTE-1154](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1154.md)) from arXiv v2 (6 June 2018, the ICML camera-ready, arXiv non-exclusive licence); worth reading for one structural condition: if the joint action-value is non-decreasing in each agent's own value, the profile of individually greedy actions is a greedy joint action, so a collective can act on a common value while each member consults only its own. The condition is sufficient, not necessary, and it cannot represent a joint value in which one agent's best action depends on what the others do at the same step. Its evidence is a two-step matrix game and StarCraft II win rates on six small maps. |
| [LIT-1504](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1504.md) | Real World Games Look Like Spinning Tops | Czarnecki, Gidel, Tracey, Tuyls, Omidshafiei, Balduzzi & Jaderberg (NeurIPS 2020). Games in which players can signal n bits before the outcome is settled contain every win–loss pattern on 2ⁿ strategies, so cycles of length 2ⁿ (Go: at least 2¹⁰⁰⁰). Nash clustering orders a game's strategies into clusters weakly ordered by population performance. Empirical games sampled from small board games and the AlphaStar league show cluster size peaking at middling strength, the "spinning top", and population-based training converges once the population is large enough. | Active — read in full 2026-10-24 ([NOTE-1146](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1146.md)) from arXiv v2 (17 June 2020); worth reading for one clean theorem, one general lemma and a hypothesis with evidence. The theorem: where players can signal n bits before the result is settled, every pattern of wins and losses among 2ⁿ strategies, a cycle through all of them included, is realized. The lemma: Nash clusters are weakly ordered by population performance, and beating a population that contains a whole cluster lifts a strategy above it. The hypothesis, that real games are shaped like a spinning top, with cycles thickest at middling strength, rests on sampled empirical games. The abstract says it is proved and the body says it is not. The random-game theorem's proof is defective, and the fixed-memory fictitious play result needs a replacement rule it does not state. |
| [LIT-1507](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1507.md) | Outrageously Large Neural Networks: The Sparsely-Gated Mixture-of-Experts Layer | Shazeer, Mirhoseini, Maziarz, Davis, Le, Hinton & Dean (2017). A layer of up to 131,072 feed-forward experts with a trainable noisy top-k gate, inserted between LSTM layers, raises capacity over 1000-fold at roughly constant computation and beat the best published language-modelling and translation results of the time. Without balancing losses the gate concentrates on a few experts, a self-reinforcing imbalance; losses penalizing unequal summed gate weight and unequal load remove it and, in one ablation, cut test perplexity from 39.8 to 35.6. | Active — read in full 2026-10-24 ([NOTE-1145](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1145.md)) from arXiv v1, the only version; worth reading here for one observation and its fix, not for its scale results. The gate of a sparsely-gated mixture of experts "tends to converge to a state where it always produces large weights for the same few experts", which the authors call self-reinforcing because favoured experts are trained more. Two auxiliary losses, the squared coefficient of variation of each expert's summed gate weight and of a smooth estimate of its load, remove the imbalance. In the one ablation (a 256-expert model, 10 epochs) no loss gives CV 3.04 and a peak-to-mean load of 17.8 at test perplexity 39.8, any loss gives 35.6–35.7. The fix equalizes use regardless of merit; the noise in the gate is there mainly to make the load estimate differentiable. |
| [LIT-1509](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1509.md) | Open-ended Learning in Symmetric Zero-sum Games | Balduzzi, Garnelo, Bachrach, Czarnecki, Pérolat, Jaderberg & Graepel (ICML 2019). Every symmetric zero-sum game between parametrized agents splits into a transitive part and a cyclic part relative to a measure on agents. In cyclic games individual performance is meaningless, so the paper measures populations, by the value of the game between them and by the convex hull of their evaluation rows (the gamescape). Response to the Nash mixture enlarges the gamescape, and response to the rectified Nash, which trains each supported agent on what it beats, grows it in Blotto-type games where self-play does not. | Active — read in full 2026-10-24 ([NOTE-1143](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1143.md)) from arXiv v2 (13 May 2019, the authors' "ICML 2019, final version"); worth reading for one invariant and one reframing. The invariant: the value of the zero-sum game between two populations, which does not depend on the choice of Nash, ignores members that are behavioural mixtures of others, and cannot be positive for a population inside another's hull. The reframing: in a cyclic game an individual agent's performance means nothing, so progress is the growth of a population's gamescape. Its functional Hodge decomposition is right but is stated with a degenerate inner product, and it depends on a measure over agents. Experiments are two small resource-allocation games. |
| [LIT-1510](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1510.md) | QTRAN: Learning to Factorize with Transformation for Cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning | Son, Kim, Kang, Hostallero & Yi define Individual-Global-Max (IGM): a joint action-value is factorised by per-agent values when the joint argmax is the profile of individual argmaxes. Additivity (VDN) and monotonicity (QMIX) are sufficient for it; QTRAN instead trains the sum of individual values plus a state value to equal the joint value at the greedy profile and to bound it elsewhere (Theorem 1), a condition also necessary up to positive rescaling. On 310 random 3×3 matrix games it learned the optimum in all, VDN and QMIX failed in 177; it also did better on Gaussian squeeze and a penalised predator-prey task. | Active — read in full 2026-10-24 ([NOTE-1141](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1141.md)) from arXiv v1 (14 May 2019, the ICML version with its supplement, arXiv non-exclusive licence); worth reading for the Individual-Global-Max condition, that the agents' individually greedy actions form a greedy joint action, and for showing it strictly weaker than additive or monotonic factorisation. The authors' own supplement notes that every single-state matrix game satisfies it, so IGM has bite only where each agent sees part of the state; it is a condition on whether members acting on local information can jointly reach the collective optimum, not a condition for a common currency. Evidence is matrix games, Gaussian squeeze and a predator-prey variant. |
| [LIT-1511](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1511.md) | Frequency adjusted multi-agent Q-learning | Kaisers & Tuyls (AAMAS 2010). The replicator-plus-entropy model of Boltzmann Q-learning derived by Tuyls et al. (2003, 2005), ẋ_i = x_i α(τ⁻¹[(Ay)_i − x·Ay] − log x_i + Σ_k x_k log x_k), assumes that every Q-value changes at rate α. In Q-learning only the chosen action's value is updated, so E[Q̇_i] carries a factor x_i, and trajectories in the prisoners' dilemma, battle of the sexes and matching pennies deviate from the model, depending on initialization. Frequency Adjusted Q-learning scales each update by min(β/x_i, 1) and follows the model wherever x_i ≥ β. | Active — read in full 2026-10-24 ([NOTE-1140](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1140.md)) from the AAMAS 2010 proceedings PDF on the IFAAMAS site; read in place of Tuyls, Verbeeck & Lenaerts 2003 ([LIT-1501](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1501.md)), whose model it restates and corrects. Worth reading as the correction to "Q-learning is replicator dynamics plus mutation": the selection–mutation equation describes Q-learning with Boltzmann exploration only if every action's estimate is updated at the same rate. In Q-learning the chosen action is updated more often, so the expected change of Q_i carries a factor x_i, and the learning traces depart from the model, depending on how the Q-values are initialized. Frequency Adjusted Q-learning divides the step by x_i and matches the model. Evidence is three 2×2 games, plotted, with no quantitative measure of fit. |
| [LIT-1512](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1512.md) | Mean Field Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning | Yang, Luo, Li, Zhou, Zhang & Wang (2018). Factorizing each agent's Q-function into pairwise terms and expanding about the neighbours' mean action reduces many-agent interaction to an agent against the average of its neighbours. Mean field Q-learning and actor-critic follow; MF-Q is proved to converge to the Nash Q-value under strong assumptions. With 500 and 1000 agents in Gaussian Squeeze the mean field methods learn where four baselines fail; MF-Q reproduces the order parameter of a 20 × 20 Ising model against MCMC; and it wins a 64-versus-64 battle game. | Active — read in full 2026-10-24 ([NOTE-1148](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1148.md)) from arXiv v5 (15 December 2020), the ICML 2018 paper with appendices; worth reading as the standard way multi-agent RL reaches hundreds of agents: each agent's Q-function takes its own action and the mean action of its neighbours, so many-body interaction becomes a two-body one between an agent and the average of the rest. Mean field Q-learning is proved to converge to a Nash Q-value under strong assumptions, every stage game met in training having a global optimum or a saddle point among them, and learns where four baselines fail with 500 and 1000 agents. The approximation needs agents that are homogeneous and interchangeable within a neighbourhood; the bound on its error is loose and the cancellation of errors argued, not proved; and the contraction step needs a high Boltzmann temperature while the convergence assumptions need it to go to zero. |
| [LIT-1513](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1513.md) | Multi-agent Reinforcement Learning in Sequential Social Dilemmas | Leibo, Zambaldi, Lanctot, Marecki & Graepel (2017). Defines a sequential social dilemma as a Markov game whose cooperative and defecting policies, played against each other, give payoffs satisfying the social dilemma inequalities. Independent deep Q-learners in a fruit-Gathering game learn aggression when apples are scarce or a tagged rival is out long; in Wolfpack they hunt together when the joint-capture bonus and radius are high. Both games embed Prisoner's Dilemmas, but network size raises defection in Gathering and lowers it in Wolfpack, which no matrix game captures. | Active — read in full 2026-10-24 ([NOTE-1151](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1151.md)) from arXiv v1, the AAMAS 2017 paper; worth reading as the paper that moved social dilemmas from matrix games to learned policies in Markov games. Two two-player games, Gathering (apples, and a beam that removes the rival for a while) and Wolfpack (lone or joint capture of prey), both yield Prisoner's Dilemma payoff matrices when the learned policies are played off, yet respond in opposite directions to agent capacity: a larger network makes Gathering agents more aggressive and Wolfpack agents more cooperative, because aggression is the harder policy to implement in one and cooperation in the other. Agents learn aggression where apples are scarce. It is a descriptive simulation with independent learners, no figures of spread, and no protective institution or depletable commons. |
| [LIT-1514](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1514.md) | Adaptive Mixtures of Local Experts | Jacobs, Jordan, Nowlan & Hinton (1991). A system of expert networks and a gating network, trained with the error of a single expert selected stochastically by the gate (or the negative log-likelihood of a mixture of Gaussians), so that each expert produces the whole output and an expert better than the gate-weighted average gains responsibility for the case. On speaker-independent vowel discrimination, 4 or 8 linear experts learned twice as fast as matched backpropagation networks at equal accuracy and divided the task by class pair; all but 2 or 3 experts went unused. | Active — read in full 2026-10-24 ([NOTE-1147](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1147.md)) from the scan of the published article on Geoffrey Hinton's University of Toronto page; worth reading as the origin of the mixture of experts and as a learning rule in which authority over a case goes to whichever expert does better than the gate-weighted average. Redefining the error as that of a single expert chosen stochastically by the gate makes the experts compete rather than cooperate, and the log-likelihood form adapts the best-fitting expert fastest. On a four-class vowel task, mixtures of 4 or 8 linear experts reached criterion in about half the epochs of backpropagation networks with matched parameters, at the same accuracy, and in every run all but 2 or 3 experts ended with mixing proportions effectively 0. The authors read that as economy; nothing in the paper tests whether the idle experts could recover. |
| [LIT-1517](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1517.md) | Counterfactual Multi-Agent Policy Gradients | Foerster, Farquhar, Afouras, Nardelli & Whiteson train decentralised actors with one centralised critic Q(s, τ, u) and credit agent a with A^a = Q(s, τ, u) − Σ_{u′a} π^a(u′a \| τ^a) Q(s, τ, (u^−a, u′a)): the value of the joint action against the critic's average over a's own alternatives under a's policy, the others' actions fixed. The baseline does not depend on a's action, so it does not change the expected gradient (Lemma 1). On decentralised StarCraft micromanagement with a narrow field of view, it beat independent and central-V/QV critics on four maps. | Active — read in full 2026-10-24 ([NOTE-1152](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1152.md)) from arXiv v3 (11 December 2024, arXiv non-exclusive licence), the corrected version; worth reading as the standard statement of counterfactual credit in cooperative multi-agent learning: each agent's action is scored against the critic's average over that agent's own alternatives, the others' actions held fixed, and that baseline provably leaves the expected gradient unchanged. The counterfactual values are the learned critic's estimates, which exist only for actions the agents sometimes take, so the method credits agents that all act on every step and does not recover the value of one that is never heeded. Results are StarCraft win rates on four small maps. |
| [LIT-1519](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1519.md) | Learning with Opponent-Learning Awareness | Foerster et al. replace an agent's objective V¹(θ¹, θ²) with its value after the opponent's anticipated naive gradient step, V¹(θ¹, θ² + Δθ²), and differentiate through Δθ² = η∇θ²V², adding (∇θ²V¹)ᵀ∇θ¹∇θ²V² · δη to the naive gradient. In the memory-one iterated prisoner's dilemma, two exact-gradient LOLA learners played tit-for-tat-like policies in 81% of runs (return −1.06 against −1.98 for naive learners); in iterated matching pennies they settled at the mixed Nash equilibrium. A policy-gradient version cooperated in the Coin Game, and with opponent modelling did so less reliably. | Active — read in full 2026-10-24 ([NOTE-1150](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1150.md)) from arXiv v4 (19 September 2018, the AAMAS 2018 text, arXiv non-exclusive licence); worth reading as the first learning rule that models another learner's update and climbs its own return through it: a LOLA agent adds to its gradient the effect of its own parameters on the opponent's next naive step. Two exact-gradient LOLA learners reached tit-for-tat-like reciprocity in the iterated prisoner's dilemma where naive learners defected. Shaping is one step deep, assumes access to the opponent's parameters (or a behavioural clone of them), and is shown only in two-player games; its numbers have one internal inconsistency (see the NOTE). |
| [LIT-1520](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1520.md) | Coupled replicator equations for the dynamics of learning in multiagent systems | Sato & Crutchfield (2002; PRE 2003). Two agents choose by softmax over reward memories Q_i that decay at rate α. In the limit where learning is slow relative to play, each agent's choice distribution follows ẋ_i/x_i = β[(Ay)_i − x·Ay] + α Σ_j x_j log(x_j/x_i): a coupled replicator dynamic plus an entropy-like term towards uniform play. With α = 0 it is the conservative two-population replicator equation; with α > 0 it is dissipative. In rock–scissors–paper, simulations show quasiperiodic tori and Hamiltonian chaos without decay, and limit cycles, intermittency and chaotic attractors with it. | Active — read in full 2026-10-24 ([NOTE-1144](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1144.md)) from arXiv:nlin/0204057v2 (18 August 2002); worth reading as a four-page derivation of the learning dynamics of softmax reinforcement learners with forgetting: two such agents follow coupled replicator equations plus a term α_X Σ_j x_j log(x_j/x_i), set by the rate at which reward memories decay, that pushes each agent towards uniform play. Without forgetting the system is conservative, Hamiltonian in zero-sum games, and in rock–scissors–paper it is chaotic for nonzero tie rewards; with forgetting it is dissipative, with limit cycles and chaotic attractors. The memory update is not Watkins's Q-learning: every action's memory is updated with its average reward at the same rate. |
| [LIT-1521](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1521.md) | A Simple Adaptive Procedure Leading to Correlated Equilibrium | Hart & Mas-Colell (Econometrica 2000; handout 1996). Regret matching: each period a player who last played j switches to k with probability R_t(j, k)/μ, the positive part of its average gain had it played k whenever it played j, and otherwise repeats j. If all players do so, the empirical distribution of play converges almost surely to the set of correlated equilibria. The proof runs through Blackwell's approachability theorem; regrets vanish exactly when the empirical distribution approaches the correlated-equilibrium set. Inertia, a positive probability of repeating, is needed for the result. | Active — read in full 2026-10-24 ([NOTE-1142](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1142.md)) from the published article as posted on Sergiu Hart's homepage; worth reading as the theorem that correlated equilibrium is reachable by simple adaptive play: if every player switches from its last action to each alternative with probability proportional to its positive regret for not having made that switch in the past, the empirical joint distribution of play converges almost surely to the set of correlated equilibria. No device, no forecasts and no best replies are needed; the common history is the correlating device. The limits matter: convergence is to the set, not to a point; correlated equilibria that are interior and not pure Nash cannot be the limit of the empirical distribution; and the players must observe one another's past play. |
| [LIT-1524](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1524.md) v2 | Cleaning up the neighborhood: A full classification for adversarial partial monitoring | Lattimore & Szepesvári (2018; ALT 2019). Completes the classification of finite adversarial partial-monitoring games by minimax regret to all games, including the degenerate ones (with actions optimal only on a lower-dimensional part of the simplex) that Bartók et al. (2014) left open: 0 with no pair of neighbouring actions, Θ̃(√n) when locally observable, Θ(n^2/3) when globally but not locally observable, and Ω(n) otherwise. A new NeighborhoodWatch2 attains √n with high probability by redistributing mass onto degenerate actions in proportion to the neighbours they lie between. It corrects a slip in Bartók et al.'s T^2/3 lower-bound proof and, in the preprint's words, an exchanged expectation and maximum in the earlier localisation argument. A second algorithm, RelExp3, gives point-locally observable games an asymptotic √n bound free of arbitrarily large game constants, with a matching linear dependence on the number of feedback symbols. | Active — read 2026-10-25 ([NOTE-1162](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1162.md)) in full, from the arXiv preprint v1 of 23 May 2018 (arxiv.org/pdf/1805.09247v1, 24 pp.); the ALT 2019 version (PMLR 98:529–556) was fetched and its theorem statements, footnote and contribution list compared, not read in full. Worth reading for the completed classification of finite adversarial partial-monitoring games, degenerate and duplicate actions included ([THEORY-963](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-963.md)); for how actions that are optimal only on a boundary enter it, through the neighbourhood set and not as neighbours, and for its correction of the lower-bound proof of Bartók et al. (2014) ([THEORY-961](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-961.md)); for NeighborhoodWatch2, a simpler algorithm with a high-probability √n bound; and for RelExp3 on point-locally observable games ([THEORY-950](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-950.md)). Read it knowing that the arXiv text says Foster and Rakhlin and Bartók et al. "inadvertently exchanged an expectation and maximum" in their localisation argument and the published text no longer says so, though both abstracts say "correct errors in previous analyses"; that it proves only the two pieces of the classification that were missing or flawed and cites the rest; that its constants are game-dependent and can be large; and that a few small typos survive in the arXiv text. |
| [LIT-1526](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1526.md) v2 | Online Learning and Blackwell Approachability with Partial Monitoring: Optimal Convergence Rates | Kwon & Perchet (2017). Blackwell approachability generalizes regret minimization (multi-criteria optimization, online optimization of a convex loss, online linear optimization under a cumulative constraint). Under partial monitoring the decision maker does not see outcomes but a random signal correlated with the decision–outcome pair, or with the outcome only. The paper gives the first approachability algorithms for polytope target sets with convergence rate O(T^-1/2) when the signal does not depend on the decision and O(T^-1/3) for general signals, and shows that these rates cannot be improved without further assumptions on the objectives or the signals (abstract). | Active — read 2026-10-25 ([NOTE-1159](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1159.md)) in full, from the PMLR copy and its supplementary material; worth reading for the reduction of approachability under partial monitoring to full-information approachability in a lifted space of flags, for the optimal worst-case rates, O(T^-1/3) for general signals and O(T^-1/2) when the signal does not depend on the decision ([THEORY-947](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-947.md)), and for the exploration floor that decision-dependent signals require ([THEORY-957](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-957.md)). Read it knowing that approachability is assumed rather than decided, that the guarantees concern the average payoff and so let violations be compensated over time, that optimality is worst case over games, that the constants grow with a simplicial subdivision, and that the proof for outcome-dependent signals is omitted. |
| [LIT-1528](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1528.md) v3 | Partial Monitoring—Classification, Regret Bounds, and Algorithms | Bartók, Foster, Pál, Rakhlin & Szepesvári (2014). In a partial-monitoring game the learner picks an action, the environment an outcome, and the learner suffers a loss and receives a feedback signal, both fixed functions of action and outcome. For every game with finitely many actions and outcomes (against adversarial opponents, every non-degenerate one) the minimax regret is zero or scales as T^1/2, T^2/3 or T, up to constants and logarithmic factors; computationally efficient algorithms attain it within a logarithmic factor, with individual bounds on expected regret for i.i.d. outcomes (abstract). | Active — read 2026-10-25 ([NOTE-1164](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1164.md)) in full, from the authors' preprint of March 2013 on Alexander Rakhlin's MIT page; worth reading for the complete classification of finite partial-monitoring games by minimax regret (0, Θ̃(√T), Θ(T^2/3), Θ(T); [THEORY-964](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-964.md)), for the linear-algebra conditions, global and local observability, that decide the class ([THEORY-962](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-962.md)), and for the algorithms CBP and NeighborhoodWatch. Read it knowing that the adversarial classification covers non-degenerate games only, that Lattimore and Szepesvári (2019, LIT-1524) completed it to degenerate games, corrected the kernel in its T^2/3 lower-bound proof, and, in their preprint, an exchanged expectation and maximum in NeighborhoodWatch's localisation (THEORY-963, THEORY-961), that the classification concerns the best policy in a fixed, known game, and that the copy read is the preprint, not the journal text. |
| [LIT-1530](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1530.md) v2 | Invariant Learning Dynamics of Transformers in Inductive Reasoning Tasks | Musat, Pimentel, Zucchet & Hofmann (2026), arXiv:2607.11875. For a class of block-list inductive tasks that includes associative recall, k-hop induction and in-context n-grams, it proves that population gradient descent keeps an idealized attention-only transformer's key–query and output weights on a low-dimensional invariant manifold fixed by the data's symmetries, whose coordinates are interpretable head actions. On it, it proves that a saturated in-weights circuit suppresses the in-context circuit's gradient by the fraction of data it does not solve and that burstiness multiplies it, shows empirically that initialization decides which of several induction circuits wins, and detects circuits in trained models by projecting onto the coordinates. | Active — read 2026-10-26 ([NOTE-1177](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1177.md)) in full, from the arXiv copy (v2); worth reading for its proof that symmetries of the data confine population gradient descent to a subspace of interpretable head actions ([THEORY-981](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-981.md)), for its theorem that a saturated memorized shortcut starves the in-context circuit of gradient on the data it solves ([THEORY-1009](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1009.md)), and for its scan in which initialization picks one of several induction circuits, read by the authors as cooperation through shared units and competition for layers ([THEORY-1001](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1001.md)). Read it knowing that the architecture is idealized (fixed orthogonal write maps, merged key-query, orthonormal embeddings), that invariance is proved and attraction is not, that the results are for gradient descent while its circuit-detection experiment uses AdamW, and that the competition scan was run in training projected onto seven coordinates. |
| [LIT-1535](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1535.md) v2 | Differentiation and Specialization of Attention Heads via the Refined Local Learning Coefficient | Wang, Hoogland, van Wingerden, Furman & Murfet (2024), arXiv:2410.02984, ICLR 2025. Refined variants of the local learning coefficient, a complexity measure from singular learning theory, are applied to individual components of a two-layer attention-only transformer, tracing how attention heads progressively differentiate into distinct functional roles during training, what data they specialize to, and a previously unidentified multigram circuit (abstract). | Active — read 2026-10-26 ([NOTE-1188](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1188.md)) in full, from the arXiv PDF of v1; worth reading as the record's first developmental use of the learning coefficient, for per-head trajectories that separate attention heads by function ([THEORY-975](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-975.md)), and for its observations of heads changing role as circuits form ([THEORY-967](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-967.md), Proposed). Read it knowing that it is one two-layer attention-only model with three appendix seeds, that the estimates are trusted only for their ordering, that cluster counts were chosen by eye, and that nothing is predicted before it happens. |
| [LIT-1538](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1538.md) v2 | In-context Learning and Induction Heads | Olsson et al. (2022), arXiv:2209.11895. Induction heads, attention heads that complete [A][B] … [A] → [B], develop at precisely the point of a sudden sharp increase in in-context learning, visible as a bump in the training loss. Six lines of evidence argue that they may be the mechanism of most in-context learning in large transformers: strong and causal for small attention-only models, correlational for larger models with MLPs (abstract). | Active — read 2026-10-26 ([NOTE-1173](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1173.md)) in full, from the arXiv print of the Transformer Circuits article; worth reading as the first mechanistic account of a transition in training, for the in-context learning score, and for the way it grades its own evidence by model class. Read it knowing that the case is causal only for small attention-only models ([THEORY-973](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-973.md)), that the large-model thesis is correlational and by analogy ([THEORY-990](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-990.md)), that every model was trained once on the same data order, and that its dates for the window disagree between sections. |
